questions.topic: Information, technologies and systems for organisational performance
questions.question_text: A mobile network operator collects millions of location pings from handsets every minute and must analyse them almost immediately to reroute traffic around congested masts. Which characteristic of big data does the need for near-instant processing best illustrate?

options.A: Volume
options.B: Velocity
options.C: Variety
options.D: Veracity

questions.explanation: Velocity refers to the speed at which data is generated and must be captured and processed, often in real time. Volume relates to the sheer quantity of data, variety to the range of formats (structured and unstructured), and veracity to the reliability or trustworthiness of the data. The emphasis here is on near-instant analysis, so velocity is the best description.

questions.topic: Information, technologies and systems for organisational performance
questions.question_text: A fashion retailer collects customer reviews from social media to gauge reaction to a new range. Many posts are sarcastic, some come from automated accounts and some are written by competitors. Which characteristic of big data does this problem relate to most directly?

options.A: Velocity
options.B: Veracity
options.C: Volume
options.D: Value

questions.explanation: Veracity concerns the accuracy, quality and trustworthiness of data. Sarcasm, bot-generated posts and deliberately misleading reviews all reduce how far the data can be relied upon. The issue is not the amount or speed of data but whether it is true, so veracity is the relevant characteristic.

questions.topic: Information, technologies and systems for organisational performance
questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of an EXTERNAL source of management information for a manufacturing company?

options.A: The company's payroll records
options.B: Industry statistics published by a trade association
options.C: Machine-hour logs from the production department
options.D: The sales ledger showing customer balances

questions.explanation: External information originates outside the organisation, such as government statistics, trade association data or competitor reports. Payroll records, machine logs and the sales ledger are all generated by the company's own systems and are therefore internal sources.

questions.topic: Information, technologies and systems for organisational performance
questions.question_text: A logistics company stores its customer database on cloud servers. Which of the following controls is designed primarily to protect the CONFIDENTIALITY of that data?

options.A: Encrypting the data both in storage and in transmission
options.B: Taking daily off-site backups of the database
options.C: Installing an uninterruptible power supply at the head office
options.D: Using check digits on customer account numbers

questions.explanation: Encryption makes data unreadable to anyone without the decryption key, so it protects confidentiality. Backups and an uninterruptible power supply protect availability, while check digits are an input control supporting data integrity (accuracy).

questions.topic: Information, technologies and systems for organisational performance
questions.question_text: The board of a hotel group wants a system that presents summarised key performance data on a dashboard, with the ability to drill down into the detail behind any figure. Which type of information system best meets this need?

options.A: A transaction processing system
options.B: An executive information system
options.C: An office automation system
options.D: An expert system

questions.explanation: An executive information system (EIS) provides senior managers with summarised internal and external information, typically via dashboards, with drill-down to underlying detail. A transaction processing system records routine transactions, office automation supports clerical tasks, and an expert system applies coded expertise to give advice on specific problems.

questions.topic: Information, technologies and systems for organisational performance
questions.question_text: A subscription software business uses three years of customer usage data to build a model that estimates the probability that each current customer will cancel during the next quarter. Which type of data analytics is this?

options.A: Descriptive analytics
options.B: Diagnostic analytics
options.C: Prescriptive analytics
options.D: Predictive analytics

questions.explanation: Predictive analytics uses historical data and statistical models to forecast what is likely to happen in future, such as the probability of a customer cancelling. Descriptive analytics summarises what has happened, diagnostic analytics explains why it happened, and prescriptive analytics recommends the action to take.

questions.topic: Information, technologies and systems for organisational performance
questions.question_text: A variance report reaches the production manager three weeks after the month end, by which time the problems it highlights have already been corrected. Which quality of good information is most clearly lacking?

options.A: Completeness
options.B: Timeliness
options.C: Accuracy
options.D: Understandability

questions.explanation: Information must be available in time for the user to act on it. A report that arrives after the problems have already been dealt with has little value even if it is accurate, complete and clear, so timeliness is the quality that is lacking.

questions.topic: Information, technologies and systems for organisational performance
questions.question_text: Which of the following best explains why traditional management accounting reports are often considered inadequate for strategic planning?

options.A: They focus mainly on internal, historical and financial data, whereas strategic planning needs external, forward-looking and non-financial information
options.B: They are produced too frequently, which causes information overload for strategic planners
options.C: They contain too much information about competitors and not enough about internal costs
options.D: They are always prepared on a cash basis rather than an accruals basis

questions.explanation: Strategic planning is long-term and outward-looking, requiring information about markets, competitors and the wider environment, much of it non-financial and uncertain. Traditional management accounting systems mainly record internal, historical financial data, which limits their usefulness for this purpose.

questions.topic: Information, technologies and systems for organisational performance
questions.question_text: A supermarket chain combines loyalty card transactions, weather forecasts and local events data. Its analysis reveals that sales of barbecue products in a region rise sharply two days after a forecast of warm weather at the weekend, and it now adjusts deliveries automatically. Which statement best describes the benefit obtained?

options.A: The data is structured, so traditional reporting would have produced the same insight at no extra cost
options.B: The benefit arises mainly from the variety of data, so velocity and volume are irrelevant to the decision
options.C: The analysis replaces the need for any management judgement in setting inventory levels
options.D: Big data analytics has identified a pattern that improves forecasting and inventory decisions

questions.explanation: Combining large, varied data sets can reveal relationships that conventional internal reports would not show, such as a lagged link between weather forecasts and product demand. Using this pattern to drive deliveries improves forecasting and reduces stock-outs and waste. The analysis supports rather than eliminates management judgement, and volume and velocity are still relevant because the data is large and must be processed quickly.

questions.question_text:
Delta Co makes two products, X and Y. Budgeted overheads are: machine set-ups $120,000; materials handling $80,000; machining $200,000.
Product X: 4,000 units, 2 machine hours per unit, 30 set-ups, 50 material movements.
Product Y: 1,000 units, 4 machine hours per unit, 50 set-ups, 110 material movements.
What is the cost driver rate for machine set-ups?

options.A: $4,000 per set-up
options.B: $1,500 per set-up
options.C: $2,400 per set-up
options.D: $10.00 per machine hour

questions.explanation: Total set-ups = 30 + 50 = 80. Cost driver rate = $120,000 / 80 = $1,500 per set-up. Dividing by only one product's set-ups, or by machine hours, would not reflect the activity that causes set-up costs.

questions.question_text:
Delta Co makes two products, X and Y. Budgeted overheads are: machine set-ups $120,000; materials handling $80,000; machining $200,000.
Product X: 4,000 units, 2 machine hours per unit, 30 set-ups, 50 material movements.
Product Y: 1,000 units, 4 machine hours per unit, 50 set-ups, 110 material movements.
Using activity-based costing, what is the overhead cost per unit of product Y (to the nearest cent)?

Delta Co makes two products, X and Y. Budgeted overheads are: machine set-ups $120,000; materials handling $80,000; machining $200,000.
Product X: 4,000 units, 2 machine hours per unit, 30 set-ups, 50 material movements.
Product Y: 1,000 units, 4 machine hours per unit, 50 set-ups, 110 material movements.
If Delta Co instead absorbed all overheads using a single factory-wide machine-hour rate, what would be the overhead cost per unit of product Y (to the nearest cent)?
questions.explanation: Total machine hours = (4,000 x 2) + (1,000 x 4) = 12,000. Overhead absorption rate = $400,000 / 12,000 = $33.3333 per machine hour. Overhead per unit of Y = 4 x $33.3333 = $133.33.

questions.question_text:
Delta Co makes two products, X and Y. Budgeted overheads are: machine set-ups $120,000; materials handling $80,000; machining $200,000.
Product X: 4,000 units, 2 machine hours per unit, 30 set-ups, 50 material movements.
Product Y: 1,000 units, 4 machine hours per unit, 50 set-ups, 110 material movements.
By how much does the overhead charged to each unit of product X under ABC differ from the overhead charged using a single factory-wide machine-hour rate (to the nearest cent)?

options.A: $15.83 higher under ABC
options.B: $63.33 lower under ABC
options.C: $63.33 higher under ABC
options.D: $15.83 lower under ABC

questions.explanation: ABC overhead for X = (30 x $1,500) + (50 x $500) + (8,000 x $16.6667) = $45,000 + $25,000 + $133,333 = $203,333, or $50.83 per unit. Machine-hour basis = 2 x $33.3333 = $66.67 per unit. ABC therefore charges $15.83 less per unit to the high-volume product X, because the low-volume product Y causes most of the set-ups and handling.

questions.question_text: In activity-based costing, what is a cost driver?

options.A: A cost that is directly attributable to a single unit of product
options.B: The factor that causes the cost of an activity to change
options.C: The cost centre to which an overhead is first allocated
options.D: The budgeted overhead divided by budgeted labour hours

questions.explanation: A cost driver is any factor whose change causes a change in the total cost of an activity, such as the number of set-ups driving set-up costs. It is not the same as a direct cost or a cost centre, and ABC deliberately avoids relying on a single labour-hour based rate.

questions.question_text: In which of the following situations is activity-based costing most likely to give significantly different product costs from traditional absorption costing?

options.A: Overheads are small and all products are made in similar batch sizes
options.B: The business makes a single standard product in long production runs
options.C: Overheads are a large proportion of total cost and products differ widely in batch sizes and complexity
options.D: Most overheads vary directly with the number of labour hours worked

questions.explanation: ABC adds most value when overheads are significant and are driven by factors other than volume, such as the number of batches, orders or design changes. If products are similar or overheads vary with labour hours, a traditional volume-based rate gives broadly similar results.

questions.question_text: Which of the following costs is most likely to be driven by the number of production batches rather than the number of units produced?

options.A: Direct materials
options.B: Power consumed while machines run
options.C: Machine set-up costs
options.D: Royalties paid per unit sold

questions.explanation: Set-up costs are incurred each time a new batch is started, regardless of how many units the batch contains, so they are batch-level costs. Direct materials, machine running power and per-unit royalties all vary with the number of units.

questions.question_text: Quality inspection costs are budgeted at $90,000 for the year, with 600 inspections expected. Product Z will be produced in a run of 2,500 units requiring 45 inspections. What is the inspection cost per unit of Z under ABC?
Which of the following is a recognised limitation of activity-based costing?

options.A: Some overheads, such as factory rent, have no clear activity driver and must still be apportioned arbitrarily
options.B: It ignores support activities and focuses only on direct labour
options.C: It can only be used in service organisations
options.D: It always produces lower product costs than absorption costing

questions.explanation: Facility-sustaining costs such as rent or the factory manager's salary are not caused by any particular product, so ABC must still spread them on an arbitrary basis. ABC also costs more to implement and maintain. It is used in both manufacturing and service organisations, and it reallocates rather than reduces total overheads.

questions.question_text: A company plans to launch a product at a market price of $80. It requires a profit margin of 25% of the selling price. The current estimated cost of the product is $68 per unit. What is the cost gap per unit?
questions.explanation: Target cost = selling price - required profit = $80 - (25% x $80) = $60. Cost gap = estimated cost - target cost = $68 - $60 = $8 per unit.

questions.question_text: A product will sell for $90. The company requires a mark-up of 25% on cost. The current estimated cost is $75 per unit. What is the cost gap per unit?
questions.explanation: With a mark-up of 25% on cost, selling price = 125% of cost. Target cost = $90 / 1.25 = $72. Cost gap = $75 - $72 = $3 per unit. Treating 25% as a margin on price would wrongly give a target cost of $67.50.

questions.question_text: What is the starting point in the target costing process?

options.A: Calculating the full production cost of the existing design
options.B: Setting a selling price that customers are expected to accept
options.C: Adding a standard mark-up to the estimated variable cost
options.D: Identifying the cost gap between estimated and actual costs

questions.explanation: Target costing is market-led: it starts with the price customers will pay, deducts the required profit to give the target cost, and then compares this with the estimated cost to find the cost gap. Cost-plus pricing starts with cost, which is the opposite approach.

questions.question_text: A cost gap has been identified for a new kitchen appliance. Which of the following actions is most consistent with closing the gap through value engineering?

options.A: Removing design features that customers do not value and using standardised components
options.B: Increasing the selling price above the market price
options.C: Reducing the required profit margin to zero
options.D: Cutting the quality of features that customers rate as most important

questions.explanation: Value engineering redesigns the product to reduce cost without reducing the value perceived by customers, for example by removing unvalued features or using common components. Raising price above the market level or abandoning the profit target defeats the purpose of target costing, and cutting valued features reduces customer value.

questions.question_text: A new product is expected to sell 50,000 units over its life. Development costs will be $400,000, total marketing costs $250,000, variable production costs $12 per unit and decommissioning costs at the end of its life $50,000. What is the life-cycle cost per unit?

A product has a three-year life. Design costs of $300,000 are incurred before launch. Expected sales and variable costs are: Year 1, 10,000 units at $8 per unit; Year 2, 25,000 units at $9 per unit; Year 3, 15,000 units at $10 per unit. Product-specific fixed production costs are $60,000 per year, and disposal costs at the end of Year 3 are $40,000. Ignoring the time value of money, what is the life-cycle cost per unit?
At which stage of a product's life are the majority of its life-cycle costs committed (locked in)?

options.A: The design and development stage
options.B: The growth stage
options.C: The maturity stage
options.D: The decline stage

questions.explanation: Design decisions about materials, components and production methods commit most of the costs that will later be incurred, even though actual spending occurs mainly during production. This is why life-cycle costing and target costing emphasise managing costs at the design stage.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a benefit of life-cycle costing compared with traditional period-based cost reporting?

options.A: Pre-production and post-production costs are attributed to the product so its total profitability over its life is visible
options.B: It removes the need to set prices that cover development costs
options.C: It treats research and development costs as period costs written off as incurred
options.D: It focuses only on the annual production costs of mature products

questions.explanation: Traditional reporting writes off research, development and decommissioning costs as period expenses, so they are not linked to the product that caused them. Life-cycle costing accumulates all costs over the product's life, helping managers judge whole-life profitability and set prices that recover all costs.

questions.question_text: During which stage of the product life cycle is a product likely to face slowing sales growth, intense price competition and a focus on cost control?

options.A: Introduction
options.B: Growth
options.C: Development
options.D: Maturity

questions.explanation: In the maturity stage, the market is saturated, sales growth slows, competitors fight for share mainly on price, and firms focus on efficiency and cost control. The introduction stage features low sales and high promotion; the growth stage features rapidly rising sales.

questions.topic: Throughput accounting and environmental management accounting
questions.question_text:
Rho Co makes product P, which sells for $50 per unit and uses $20 of direct materials per unit. Each unit needs 0.5 hours on the bottleneck machine. Total factory costs (all labour and overheads) are $600,000 per year and 25,000 bottleneck hours are available per year.
What is the throughput return per bottleneck hour for product P?
questions.explanation: Throughput per unit = selling price - direct materials = $50 - $20 = $30. Return per bottleneck hour = $30 / 0.5 hours = $60.

questions.topic: Throughput accounting and environmental management accounting
questions.question_text:
Rho Co makes product P, which sells for $50 per unit and uses $20 of direct materials per unit. Each unit needs 0.5 hours on the bottleneck machine. Total factory costs (all labour and overheads) are $600,000 per year and 25,000 bottleneck hours are available per year.
What is the throughput accounting ratio (TPAR) for product P?
questions.explanation: Return per factory hour = ($50 - $20) / 0.5 = $60. Cost per factory hour = $600,000 / 25,000 = $24. TPAR = $60 / $24 = 2.50. A TPAR above 1 means the product generates more throughput than it costs to run the factory for the time it uses.

questions.topic: Throughput accounting and environmental management accounting
questions.question_text: In throughput accounting, how is throughput defined?

options.A: Sales revenue less all variable costs
options.B: Sales revenue less direct material costs
options.C: Sales revenue less direct material and direct labour costs
options.D: Contribution less fixed production overheads

questions.explanation: Throughput accounting treats only direct materials as truly variable. Throughput is therefore sales revenue minus direct material cost; labour and overheads are treated as fixed factory costs.

questions.topic: Throughput accounting and environmental management accounting
questions.question_text: A product currently has a throughput accounting ratio of 0.9. Which of the following actions would improve its TPAR?

options.A: Paying overtime to non-bottleneck staff to increase their output
options.B: Reducing the selling price of the product
options.C: Negotiating a lower price for the product's direct materials
options.D: Building up inventory at non-bottleneck stages of production

questions.explanation: TPAR = (throughput per bottleneck hour) / (factory cost per hour). Lower material prices increase throughput per unit and so raise the ratio. Overtime at non-bottleneck stages adds cost without increasing output through the bottleneck, a lower price reduces throughput, and extra inventory ties up cash without increasing sales.

questions.topic: Throughput accounting and environmental management accounting
questions.question_text:
Sigma Co has a bottleneck in its painting process. Details of three products are:
Product A: price $40, direct materials $16, painting time 12 minutes
Product B: price $55, direct materials $25, painting time 20 minutes
Product C: price $30, direct materials $6, painting time 15 minutes
Using throughput accounting, in what order should the products be ranked for production?

options.A: B, A, C
options.B: C, A, B
options.C: A, B, C
options.D: A, C, B

questions.explanation: Throughput per bottleneck hour: A = ($40 - $16) / (12/60) = $120; B = ($55 - $25) / (20/60) = $90; C = ($30 - $6) / (15/60) = $96. Ranking by return per bottleneck hour gives A ($120), C ($96), then B ($90). Ranking by throughput per unit would wrongly put B first.

questions.topic: Throughput accounting and environmental management accounting
questions.question_text: According to the theory of constraints, what is the first of the five focusing steps?

options.A: Elevate the bottleneck by buying extra capacity
options.B: Subordinate all other processes to the bottleneck
options.C: Decide how to exploit the bottleneck
options.D: Identify the system's bottleneck

questions.explanation: The five focusing steps are: identify the constraint, decide how to exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it, and then return to step one if the constraint has moved. Elevating the constraint by investing in capacity comes only after the existing capacity has been fully exploited.

questions.topic: Throughput accounting and environmental management accounting
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is consistent with the principles of throughput accounting?

options.A: Inventory should be built up at every stage of production to protect output
options.B: Work in progress is valued at full absorption cost to boost reported profit
options.C: Products should be ranked according to their contribution per unit
options.D: Direct labour costs are treated as part of fixed factory costs

questions.explanation: Throughput accounting assumes labour is a fixed cost in the short term, so all costs other than materials are fixed factory costs. It discourages building inventory except before the bottleneck, values inventory at material cost only, and ranks products by throughput per bottleneck unit rather than per unit.

questions.topic: Throughput accounting and environmental management accounting
questions.question_text: An environmental management accounting technique records all physical inputs of materials and energy, and balances them against outputs of finished products, waste and emissions, so that unexplained differences can be investigated. What is this technique?

options.A: Life-cycle costing
options.B: Input/output analysis
options.C: Activity-based costing
options.D: Environmental impact assessment

questions.explanation: Input/output analysis operates on the principle that what comes in must go out: physical inputs are balanced against product outputs and waste. Any difference highlights material losses or unrecorded waste that can be costed and reduced. Flow cost accounting extends this idea by valuing the material flows.

questions.topic: Throughput accounting and environmental management accounting
questions.question_text: A chemical company estimates the compensation and clean-up costs that might arise if an accidental spill from its plant polluted a nearby river. Using the US Environmental Protection Agency classification of environmental costs, how would these costs be classified?

options.A: Contingent costs
options.B: Conventional costs
options.C: Image and relationship costs
options.D: Potentially hidden costs

questions.explanation: Contingent costs are costs that may be incurred at a future date depending on events, such as fines, compensation and remediation after an accident. Conventional costs are ordinary operating costs such as materials and energy, potentially hidden costs are buried in general overheads, and image and relationship costs relate to stakeholders' perceptions.

questions.topic: Throughput accounting and environmental management accounting
questions.question_text: Using Hansen and Mendoza's classification of environmental costs, the cost of cleaning up a lake that has been polluted by a factory's waste water would be classified as which type of cost?

options.A: External failure cost
options.B: Prevention cost
options.C: Detection cost
options.D: Internal failure cost

questions.explanation: External failure costs arise after contaminants have been released into the environment, for example cleaning a polluted lake. Prevention costs are incurred to stop waste being produced, detection costs check compliance, and internal failure costs are incurred to deal with waste that has been produced but not yet released.

questions.question_text:
Kappa Co sells two products in the constant unit ratio of 3 units of A to 2 units of B. Product A sells for $20 with variable cost of $12 per unit. Product B sells for $30 with variable cost of $15 per unit. Fixed costs are $186,000 per period.
What is the weighted average contribution to sales ratio?
questions.explanation: For a batch of 3 A and 2 B: contribution = (3 x $8) + (2 x $15) = $54; revenue = (3 x $20) + (2 x $30) = $120. Weighted average C/S ratio = $54 / $120 = 45%. Weighting the individual C/S ratios (40% and 50%) by units sold, rather than by revenue, gives the wrong answer of 44%.

questions.question_text:
Kappa Co sells two products in the constant unit ratio of 3 units of A to 2 units of B. Product A sells for $20 with variable cost of $12 per unit. Product B sells for $30 with variable cost of $15 per unit. Fixed costs are $186,000 per period.
What is the breakeven sales revenue (to the nearest $)?
questions.explanation: Weighted average C/S ratio = $54 / $120 = 0.45. Breakeven revenue = fixed costs / C/S ratio = $186,000 / 0.45 = $413,333 (rounded).

questions.question_text:
Kappa Co sells two products in the constant unit ratio of 3 units of A to 2 units of B. Product A sells for $20 with variable cost of $12 per unit. Product B sells for $30 with variable cost of $15 per unit. Fixed costs are $186,000 per period.
How many units of product B must be sold to break even (to the nearest unit)?

options.A: 10,333 units
options.B: 6,889 units
options.C: 17,222 units
options.D: 8,611 units

questions.explanation: Contribution per batch (3A + 2B) = $54. Breakeven batches = $186,000 / $54 = 3444.44. Units of B = 3444.44 x 2 = 6,889 units (rounded). Units of A would be 10,333.

questions.question_text:
Kappa Co sells two products in the constant unit ratio of 3 units of A to 2 units of B. Product A sells for $20 with variable cost of $12 per unit. Product B sells for $30 with variable cost of $15 per unit. Fixed costs are $186,000 per period.
Budgeted sales revenue, in the standard mix, is $500,000. What is the margin of safety as a percentage of budgeted sales (to one decimal place)?
questions.explanation: Breakeven revenue = $186,000 / 0.45 = $413,333. Margin of safety = ($500,000 - $413,333) / $500,000 = 17.3%. The margin of safety is always expressed relative to budgeted sales, not breakeven sales.

questions.question_text:
Kappa Co sells two products in the constant unit ratio of 3 units of A to 2 units of B. Product A sells for $20 with variable cost of $12 per unit. Product B sells for $30 with variable cost of $15 per unit. Fixed costs are $186,000 per period.
What sales revenue is needed, in the standard mix, to earn a profit of $45,000 (to the nearest $)?
questions.explanation: Required contribution = fixed costs + target profit = $186,000 + $45,000 = $231,000. Required revenue = $231,000 / 0.45 = $513,333 (rounded). Simply adding the profit to breakeven revenue ignores the fact that each $1 of sales only adds $0.45 of contribution.

questions.question_text: A company prepares a multi-product profit-volume chart that plots each product individually. In what order should the products be plotted?

options.A: In order of decreasing sales revenue
options.B: In order of increasing contribution per unit
options.C: In order of decreasing contribution to sales ratio, starting with the highest
options.D: In alphabetical order of product name

questions.explanation: On a multi-product P/V chart the products are plotted in order of their C/S ratios, highest first, so the line rises most steeply at the start. This produces a bow-shaped line above the straight line joining the start and end points, which represents the average mix.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an assumption underlying multi-product cost-volume-profit analysis?

options.A: The sales mix remains constant at all levels of activity
options.B: Fixed costs increase in steps as activity rises
options.C: Selling prices fall as more units are sold
options.D: Variable cost per unit changes with the volume of output

questions.explanation: Multi-product CVP analysis uses a weighted average contribution, which is only valid if products are sold in a constant mix. It also assumes constant selling prices, constant variable costs per unit and fixed costs that do not change within the relevant range.

questions.question_text: On a traditional breakeven chart, which of the following is true?

options.A: The total cost line starts at the origin
options.B: The sales revenue line starts at the level of fixed costs
options.C: Profit is measured by the vertical distance between the fixed cost line and the sales revenue line
options.D: The fixed cost line is drawn parallel to the horizontal (activity) axis

questions.explanation: Fixed costs do not change with activity, so they are shown as a horizontal line. The total cost line starts at the fixed cost level on the vertical axis, the revenue line starts at the origin, and profit is the vertical gap between total revenue and total cost to the right of the breakeven point.

questions.question_text: A company sells two products. Product M has a contribution to sales ratio of 30% and product N a ratio of 55%. If the sales mix shifts towards product N while total revenue and fixed costs are unchanged, what will happen?

options.A: The breakeven revenue will fall
options.B: The breakeven revenue will rise
options.C: The breakeven revenue will not change because fixed costs are unchanged
options.D: Profit will fall because the mix has changed

questions.explanation: Shifting the mix towards the product with the higher C/S ratio increases the weighted average C/S ratio. Breakeven revenue equals fixed costs divided by the weighted C/S ratio, so it falls, and profit at the same total revenue rises.

questions.question_text: A single-product company sells its product for $45 with variable cost of $27 per unit. Fixed costs are $108,000 and budgeted sales are 7,500 units. What is the margin of safety as a percentage of budgeted sales?
questions.explanation: Contribution per unit = $45 - $27 = $18. Breakeven = $108,000 / $18 = 6,000 units. Margin of safety = (7,500 - 6,000) / 7,500 = 20%.

questions.question_text:
Tau Co makes three products. Labour is limited to 12,000 hours next period.
Product X: contribution $24 per unit, 3 labour hours per unit, maximum demand 2,000 units
Product Y: contribution $30 per unit, 5 labour hours per unit, maximum demand 1,500 units
Product Z: contribution $21 per unit, 2 labour hours per unit, maximum demand 1,000 units
In what order should the products be ranked to maximise contribution?

options.A: Y, X, Z
options.B: X, Z, Y
options.C: Y, Z, X
options.D: Z, X, Y

questions.explanation: Contribution per labour hour: X = $24 / 3 = $8.00; Y = $30 / 5 = $6.00; Z = $21 / 2 = $10.50. With labour as the limiting factor, products are ranked by contribution per hour: Z, X, then Y. Ranking by contribution per unit would wrongly put Y first.

questions.question_text:
Tau Co makes three products. Labour is limited to 12,000 hours next period.
Product X: contribution $24 per unit, 3 labour hours per unit, maximum demand 2,000 units
Product Y: contribution $30 per unit, 5 labour hours per unit, maximum demand 1,500 units
Product Z: contribution $21 per unit, 2 labour hours per unit, maximum demand 1,000 units
How many units of product Y will be made in the optimal plan?

options.A: 800 units
options.B: 1,500 units
options.C: 2,400 units
options.D: 1,200 units

questions.explanation: Make Z first: 1,000 units x 2 hours = 2,000 hours. Then X: 2,000 units x 3 hours = 6,000 hours. Hours remaining = 12,000 - 2,000 - 6,000 = 4,000. Units of Y = 4,000 / 5 = 800 units. Omitting Z and making only X before Y would wrongly leave 6,000 hours for 1,200 units of Y.

questions.question_text:
Tau Co makes three products. Labour is limited to 12,000 hours next period.
Product X: contribution $24 per unit, 3 labour hours per unit, maximum demand 2,000 units
Product Y: contribution $30 per unit, 5 labour hours per unit, maximum demand 1,500 units
Product Z: contribution $21 per unit, 2 labour hours per unit, maximum demand 1,000 units
What is the maximum contribution that Tau Co can earn next period?

Omega Co makes products X and Y. Contribution is $40 per unit of X and $50 per unit of Y. Constraints are:
Labour: 2x + 4y <= 4,000 hours
Machine: 3x + 2y <= 3,600 hours
Demand for X: x <= 1,000 units
where x and y are the units of X and Y produced.
What is the optimal production plan?

options.A: 1,000 units of X and 300 units of Y
options.B: 0 units of X and 1,000 units of Y
options.C: 800 units of X and 600 units of Y
options.D: 1,000 units of X and 500 units of Y

questions.explanation: Solving the binding labour and machine constraints simultaneously: from 2x + 4y = 4,000, x = 2,000 - 2y; substituting into 3x + 2y = 3,600 gives 6,000 - 4y = 3,600, so y = 600 and x = 800. Contribution at the vertices is: (0, 1,000) $50,000; (800, 600) $62,000; (1,000, 300) $55,000; (1,000, 0) $40,000. The optimum is 800 X and 600 Y. The combination 1,000 X and 500 Y breaches the machine constraint.

questions.question_text:
Omega Co makes products X and Y. Contribution is $40 per unit of X and $50 per unit of Y. Constraints are:
Labour: 2x + 4y <= 4,000 hours
Machine: 3x + 2y <= 3,600 hours
Demand for X: x <= 1,000 units
where x and y are the units of X and Y produced.
What is the shadow price of one labour hour?
questions.explanation: Adding one labour hour and solving 2x + 4y = 4,001 with 3x + 2y = 3,600 gives x = 799.75, y = 600.375. New contribution = (40 x 799.75) + (50 x 600.375) = $62,008.75, an increase of $8.75. Equivalently, solving 2L + 3M = 40 and 4L + 2M = 50 gives L = $8.75 and M = $7.50.

questions.question_text: In linear programming, what does the shadow price of a scarce resource represent?

options.A: The normal purchase price of one unit of the resource
options.B: The contribution earned per unit of the product that uses most of the resource
options.C: The amount of the resource that remains unused in the optimal solution
options.D: The increase in total contribution if one extra unit of the resource were available, which is the maximum premium worth paying above its normal cost

questions.explanation: The shadow price (dual price) is the change in the objective function from one additional unit of a binding constraint. It is the most a business should pay over and above the normal cost for an extra unit. The unused amount of a resource is called slack.

questions.question_text: In the optimal solution to a linear programming problem, machine hours are not fully used. Which of the following is true of the machine-hour constraint?

options.A: It has slack and its shadow price is zero
options.B: It has slack and a positive shadow price
options.C: It has no slack and its shadow price is zero
options.D: It is binding and must be relaxed to increase contribution

questions.explanation: A constraint that is not fully used is non-binding: it has slack (unused capacity). Obtaining more of a resource that is already in surplus cannot increase contribution, so its shadow price is zero.

questions.question_text: When solving a two-product linear programming problem graphically, how is the optimal point identified?

options.A: By choosing the vertex of the feasible region closest to the origin
options.B: By finding where the iso-contribution line crosses the horizontal axis
options.C: By selecting the point where the demand constraint meets the vertical axis
options.D: By moving the iso-contribution line away from the origin until it last touches the feasible region

questions.explanation: The iso-contribution line joins all combinations giving the same contribution and has a slope set by the products' relative contributions. Moving it outwards, parallel to itself, increases contribution; the last point of the feasible region it touches is the optimal solution, usually a vertex.

questions.question_text:
Omega Co makes products X and Y. Contribution is $40 per unit of X and $50 per unit of Y. Constraints are:
Labour: 2x + 4y <= 4,000 hours
Machine: 3x + 2y <= 3,600 hours
Demand for X: x <= 1,000 units
where x and y are the units of X and Y produced.
The shadow price of labour has been calculated as $8.75 per hour. Additional labour hours could be obtained by paying an overtime premium of $10 per hour above the normal rate. What should Omega Co do?

options.A: Buy the extra hours, because labour is a binding constraint
options.B: Not buy the extra hours, because the premium exceeds the extra contribution each hour would generate
options.C: Buy the extra hours, because the premium is less than the contribution per unit of Y
options.D: Not buy the extra hours, because labour has slack in the optimal solution

questions.explanation: Each additional labour hour increases contribution by the shadow price of $8.75 (before the premium). Paying a premium of $10 would reduce profit by $1.25 per hour, so it is not worthwhile even though labour is binding. Comparing the premium with contribution per unit rather than per hour is a common error.

questions.question_text: Psi Co makes products X and Y. Each unit of X uses 2 kg of material M and each unit of Y uses 5 kg. Only 10,000 kg of material M are available. Each unit of X earns contribution of $12 and each unit of Y $25. If x and y are the units produced, which of the following correctly states the material constraint?
questions.explanation: Each unit of X uses 2 kg and each unit of Y uses 5 kg, so total material used is 2x + 5y, which cannot exceed the 10,000 kg available. Contribution figures belong in the objective function (maximise 12x + 25y), not in the resource constraint.

questions.question_text:
Phi Co currently sells 2,000 units of a product per month at $100 each. Market research shows that for every $5 increase in price, demand falls by 100 units (and vice versa). The variable cost is $40 per unit and fixed costs are unaffected by volume.
In the demand equation P = a - bQ, what is the value of a?
questions.explanation: b = change in price / change in quantity = $5 / 100 = 0.05. Substituting P = 100 and Q = 2,000: 100 = a - (0.05 x 2,000), so a = 100 + 100 = $200. This is the price at which demand would fall to zero.

questions.question_text:
Phi Co currently sells 2,000 units of a product per month at $100 each. Market research shows that for every $5 increase in price, demand falls by 100 units (and vice versa). The variable cost is $40 per unit and fixed costs are unaffected by volume.
Which equation gives marginal revenue (MR)?
questions.explanation: If P = a - bQ, then MR = a - 2bQ. Here P = 200 - 0.05Q, so MR = 200 - 0.1Q. The MR line has the same intercept as the demand curve but twice the slope.

questions.question_text:
Phi Co currently sells 2,000 units of a product per month at $100 each. Market research shows that for every $5 increase in price, demand falls by 100 units (and vice versa). The variable cost is $40 per unit and fixed costs are unaffected by volume.
What is the profit-maximising selling price?
questions.explanation: Demand: P = 200 - 0.05Q, so MR = 200 - 0.1Q. Profit is maximised where MR = MC: 200 - 0.1Q = 40, giving Q = 1,600. Price = 200 - (0.05 x 1,600) = $120.

questions.question_text:
Phi Co currently sells 2,000 units of a product per month at $100 each. Market research shows that for every $5 increase in price, demand falls by 100 units (and vice versa). The variable cost is $40 per unit and fixed costs are unaffected by volume.
What is the maximum monthly contribution that can be earned?
questions.explanation: Optimal output is 1,600 units at $120 (where MR = MC). Contribution = ($120 - $40) x 1,600 = $128,000, compared with $120,000 at the current price.

questions.question_text: In which of the following circumstances is a price skimming strategy most appropriate?

options.A: The product is new and innovative, and early buyers are prepared to pay a high price
options.B: The market is highly price-sensitive and competitors can easily copy the product
options.C: The company wants to gain a large market share as quickly as possible
options.D: The product is a mature commodity sold in a crowded market

questions.explanation: Price skimming sets a high initial price to exploit customers who value novelty and are not price-sensitive, recovering development costs quickly. It works best where the product is new and differentiated and barriers to entry protect it for a time. Penetration pricing suits price-sensitive markets and rapid share growth.

questions.question_text: A company launches a new streaming service at a very low monthly price, intending to build a large customer base quickly and discourage competitors from entering. Which pricing strategy is this?

options.A: Price skimming
options.B: Premium pricing
options.C: Complementary product pricing
options.D: Penetration pricing

questions.explanation: Penetration pricing sets a low initial price to win market share quickly, gain economies of scale and deter new entrants. Skimming and premium pricing use high prices, while complementary product pricing links the prices of products that are used together.

questions.question_text: A company increases the price of its product by 10%, and the quantity sold falls by 25%. Which of the following is correct?

options.A: Demand is price elastic and total revenue falls by 17.5%
options.B: Demand is price inelastic and total revenue rises by 7.5%
options.C: Demand is price elastic and total revenue falls by 15%
options.D: Demand is price inelastic and total revenue falls by 17.5%

questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand = % change in quantity / % change in price = -25% / 10% = -2.5. Its absolute value exceeds 1, so demand is elastic. New revenue = 1.10 x 0.75 = 0.825 of the original, a fall of 17.5%.

questions.question_text: A product has a full cost of $64 per unit, of which $40 is variable. The company sets prices using full cost plus 25%. What mark-up on variable cost would give the same selling price?
questions.explanation: Selling price = $64 x 1.25 = $80. Mark-up on variable cost = ($80 - $40) / $40 = 100%.

questions.question_text: Which of the following conditions is necessary for a price discrimination strategy to be effective?

options.A: All customers must have the same price elasticity of demand
options.B: The product must be sold at a single price in all markets
options.C: The cost of separating the segments must exceed the extra revenue gained
options.D: The market can be divided into segments with different price elasticities, and customers cannot easily resell between segments

questions.explanation: Price discrimination charges different prices to different groups for the same product. It only works if segments have different sensitivities to price, if they can be kept apart so low-price buyers cannot resell to high-price buyers, and if the cost of separating them is less than the extra revenue.

questions.question_text: Chi Co sells 12,000 units per month of a product at $60 each. Each $2 reduction in price would increase demand by 800 units per month. The variable cost is $20 per unit. What is the profit-maximising price?

questions.topic: Make or buy and other short-term decisions
questions.question_text: Which of the following best defines a relevant cost for decision-making?

options.A: A future, incremental cash flow that arises as a direct result of the decision
options.B: Any cost recorded in the accounting records for the period
options.C: A cost that has already been incurred and cannot be recovered
options.D: A share of general fixed overheads apportioned to the decision

questions.explanation: Relevant costs are future, cash-based and incremental: they change as a result of the decision being taken. Sunk costs, committed costs and apportioned fixed overheads that will be incurred anyway are not relevant.

questions.topic: Make or buy and other short-term decisions
questions.question_text: A one-off contract requires 800 kg of material K. The company holds 500 kg of K in inventory, bought for $4.00 per kg. The current replacement cost is $5.20 per kg and the resale value is $3.10 per kg. Material K is used regularly in the company's normal production. What is the relevant cost of material K for the contract?
questions.explanation: Because K is in regular use, any inventory used on the contract must be replaced, so all 800 kg are valued at replacement cost. Relevant cost = 800 x $5.20 = $4,160. The historical cost of $4.00 is a sunk cost.

questions.topic: Make or buy and other short-term decisions
questions.question_text: A one-off contract requires 800 kg of material K. The company holds 500 kg of K in inventory, bought for $4.00 per kg. The current replacement cost is $5.20 per kg and the resale value is $3.10 per kg. Material K is NOT used for any other purpose, and if not used on the contract the inventory would be sold. What is the relevant cost of material K for the contract?
questions.explanation: The 500 kg in inventory would otherwise be sold, so their relevant cost is the lost resale value: 500 x $3.10 = $1,550. The remaining 300 kg must be bought at $5.20: 300 x $5.20 = $1,560. Total relevant cost = $3,110.

questions.topic: Make or buy and other short-term decisions
questions.question_text: A special order needs 200 hours of skilled labour. Skilled workers are paid $15 per hour and are fully employed making product Q, which earns a contribution of $12 per labour hour after charging labour costs. If the order is accepted, production of Q will be reduced. What is the relevant cost of the skilled labour for the order?
questions.explanation: Labour is scarce, so diverting it to the order costs both the wage and the contribution lost from product Q. Relevant cost per hour = $15 + $12 = $27. Total = 200 x $27 = $5,400. Adding the wage on top of a contribution figure that already includes it ($15 + $27 = $42 per hour, giving $8,400) double-counts the labour cost.

questions.topic: Make or buy and other short-term decisions
questions.question_text: A company spent $35,000 last month on market research into a possible new product. When deciding whether to launch the product, how should the $35,000 be treated?

options.A: Included in full as a cost of the launch
options.B: Included only if the product is launched
options.C: Spread over the expected life of the product as a relevant cost
options.D: Ignored, because it is a sunk cost

questions.explanation: The market research has already been paid for and will not change whatever decision is made. It is a sunk cost and is therefore irrelevant to the launch decision.

questions.topic: Make or buy and other short-term decisions
questions.question_text: A company makes 10,000 units per year of a component at a variable cost of $18 per unit. Specific fixed costs of $40,000 per year would be avoided if the component were bought in, and general fixed overheads of $30,000 are currently absorbed into the component's cost. An outside supplier offers the component at $21 per unit. What should the company do?

options.A: Make the component, saving $30,000 per year
options.B: Make the component, saving $10,000 per year
options.C: Buy the component, saving $10,000 per year
options.D: Buy the component, saving $40,000 per year

questions.explanation: Relevant cost of making = (10,000 x $18) + $40,000 avoidable fixed costs = $220,000. Cost of buying = 10,000 x $21 = $210,000. Buying saves $10,000 per year. The $30,000 of general overheads is unavoidable and therefore irrelevant.

questions.topic: Make or buy and other short-term decisions
questions.question_text:
A company needs both components P and Q but has insufficient labour hours to make all its requirements, so it must buy in some units. Details per unit are:
Component P: variable cost to make $14, price to buy $20, labour 2 hours
Component Q: variable cost to make $10, price to buy $18, labour 4 hours
Which component should be bought in first, and why?

options.A: Component P, because its extra cost of buying is only $6 per unit
options.B: Component Q, because its variable cost of making is lower
options.C: Component Q, because the extra cost of buying is only $2.00 per labour hour saved
options.D: Component P, because the extra cost of buying is only $3.00 per labour hour saved

questions.explanation: When labour is scarce, buy the component with the lowest extra cost per hour of labour saved. P: ($20 - $14) / 2 hours = $3.00 per hour. Q: ($18 - $10) / 4 hours = $2.00 per hour. Q should be bought first, even though its extra cost per unit ($8) is higher than P's ($6).

questions.topic: Make or buy and other short-term decisions
questions.question_text: A division of a retail chain reports annual contribution of $30,000. Its fixed costs comprise $45,000 that would be avoided if it closed and $25,000 of head office costs that would continue regardless. If the division is closed, what will happen to the company's annual profit?

options.A: It will decrease by $30,000
options.B: It will increase by $40,000
options.C: It will increase by $15,000
options.D: It will decrease by $10,000

questions.explanation: Closing the division loses $30,000 of contribution but saves $45,000 of avoidable fixed costs. Profit therefore rises by $45,000 - $30,000 = $15,000. The $25,000 of head office costs is unavoidable and irrelevant.

questions.topic: Make or buy and other short-term decisions
questions.question_text: A joint product can be sold at the split-off point for $6.00 per kg. Alternatively it can be processed further at an incremental cost of $2.50 per kg and sold for $9.20 per kg. Joint costs are allocated at $3.00 per kg. Output is 10,000 kg. What is the effect of processing further?

options.A: Profit increases by $7,000
options.B: Profit decreases by $23,000
options.C: Profit increases by $67,000
options.D: Profit increases by $32,000

questions.explanation: Incremental revenue = $9.20 - $6.00 = $3.20 per kg; incremental cost = $2.50 per kg. Gain = $0.70 x 10,000 = $7,000, so the product should be processed further. Joint costs are incurred whatever the decision and are irrelevant.

questions.topic: Make or buy and other short-term decisions
questions.question_text: A manufacturer is considering outsourcing the production of a key component to an overseas supplier at a lower cost. Which of the following is a non-financial factor that should be considered?

options.A: The difference between the supplier's price and the internal variable cost
options.B: The avoidable fixed costs of in-house production
options.C: The contribution that the released capacity could earn on other work
options.D: The reliability of supply and the consistency of quality from the supplier

questions.explanation: Price differences, avoidable fixed costs and the opportunity cost of freed capacity are all financial factors included in the relevant cost calculation. Supply reliability, quality, loss of skills and confidentiality are qualitative factors that are harder to quantify but can be decisive.

questions.question_text:
A bakery must decide the size of a daily order: small, medium or large. Daily demand may be low (probability 0.3), medium (probability 0.5) or high (probability 0.2). Profits ($) for each combination are:
Small order: low 40, medium 40, high 40
Medium order: low 20, medium 60, high 60
Large order: low -10, medium 45, high 100
Which order size would be chosen using the maximax criterion?

options.A: Large
options.B: Small
options.C: Medium
options.D: Medium or large equally

questions.explanation: Maximax selects the option with the highest possible payoff. The best outcomes are: small $40, medium $60, large $100. The large order offers the highest maximum, so an optimistic decision-maker would choose it.

questions.question_text:
A bakery must decide the size of a daily order: small, medium or large. Daily demand may be low (probability 0.3), medium (probability 0.5) or high (probability 0.2). Profits ($) for each combination are:
Small order: low 40, medium 40, high 40
Medium order: low 20, medium 60, high 60
Large order: low -10, medium 45, high 100
Which order size would be chosen using expected values, and what is its expected profit?

options.A: Large, with expected profit of $39.50
options.B: Medium, with expected profit of $48
options.C: Small, with expected profit of $40
options.D: Large, with expected profit of $45.00

questions.explanation: EV small = $40. EV medium = (0.3 x 20) + (0.5 x 60) + (0.2 x 60) = $48. EV large = (0.3 x -10) + (0.5 x 45) + (0.2 x 100) = $39.50. The medium order has the highest EV.

questions.question_text:
A bakery must decide the size of a daily order: small, medium or large. Daily demand may be low (probability 0.3), medium (probability 0.5) or high (probability 0.2). Profits ($) for each combination are:
Small order: low 40, medium 40, high 40
Medium order: low 20, medium 60, high 60
Large order: low -10, medium 45, high 100
Which order size would be chosen using the maximin criterion?

options.A: Small
options.B: Medium
options.C: Large
options.D: Small or medium equally

questions.explanation: Maximin selects the option whose worst outcome is the best. Worst outcomes: small $40, medium $20, large -$10. The small order has the highest minimum, so a pessimistic or risk-averse decision-maker would choose it.

questions.question_text:
A bakery must decide the size of a daily order: small, medium or large. Daily demand may be low (probability 0.3), medium (probability 0.5) or high (probability 0.2). Profits ($) for each combination are:
Small order: low 40, medium 40, high 40
Medium order: low 20, medium 60, high 60
Large order: low -10, medium 45, high 100
Which order size would be chosen using the minimax regret criterion?

options.A: Small
options.B: Large
options.C: Small or large equally
options.D: Medium

questions.explanation: Best payoff for each demand level: low 40, medium 60, high 100. Regrets: small 0, 20, 60 (maximum 60); medium 20, 0, 40 (maximum 40); large 50, 15, 0 (maximum 50). The lowest maximum regret is 40, for the medium order.

questions.question_text:
A bakery must decide the size of a daily order: small, medium or large. Daily demand may be low (probability 0.3), medium (probability 0.5) or high (probability 0.2). Profits ($) for each combination are:
Small order: low 40, medium 40, high 40
Medium order: low 20, medium 60, high 60
Large order: low -10, medium 45, high 100
What is the expected value of perfect information about daily demand?
questions.explanation: With perfect information the bakery would choose the best order for each demand level: EV = (0.3 x 40) + (0.5 x 60) + (0.2 x 100) = $62. Without information the best EV is $48. EVPI = $62 - $48 = $14, the maximum worth paying for a perfect demand forecast.

questions.question_text: A manager always chooses the option with the best worst-case outcome. Which attitude to risk and decision criterion does this indicate?

options.A: Risk-seeking, using the maximax criterion
options.B: Risk-neutral, using expected values
options.C: Risk-seeking, using the minimax regret criterion
options.D: Risk-averse, using the maximin criterion

questions.explanation: Choosing the option whose worst outcome is least bad reflects a pessimistic, risk-averse attitude and is the maximin rule. Maximax suits a risk-seeker, and expected values suit a risk-neutral decision-maker.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a limitation of using expected values for decision-making?

options.A: The expected value may not correspond to any actual outcome, so it is less reliable for one-off decisions
options.B: It cannot be used when probabilities are known
options.C: It takes too much account of the decision-maker's attitude to risk
options.D: It considers only the worst possible outcome of each option

questions.explanation: An expected value is a long-run average; it is most meaningful for decisions repeated many times. For a one-off decision the actual result will be one of the possible outcomes, not the EV. It also ignores the decision-maker's attitude to risk and depends on reliable probability estimates.

questions.question_text: A company is deciding whether to launch a product at a cost of $100,000. There is a 0.6 probability of success, giving a return of $300,000. If the launch fails (probability 0.4), the company can either abandon the product and sell the equipment for $50,000, or spend $30,000 modifying it, in which case there is a 0.5 probability of a return of $200,000 and a 0.5 probability of a return of $20,000. All values are in present value terms. What is the expected value of launching the product, assuming the best choice is made at each decision point?
questions.explanation: Roll back from the right. If the launch fails: modifying gives (0.5 x $200,000) + (0.5 x $20,000) - $30,000 = $80,000, which exceeds the $50,000 from abandoning, so modify. EV of launch = (0.6 x $300,000) + (0.4 x $80,000) - $100,000 = $112,000.

questions.question_text: A project has a net present value of $50,000. The present value of sales revenue is $400,000. By what percentage could the selling price fall before the project's NPV becomes zero (the sensitivity of the project to selling price)?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = NPV / PV of the cash flow concerned = $50,000 / $400,000 = 12.5%. If selling prices fell by more than 12.5%, the NPV would become negative, assuming all other variables are unchanged.

questions.question_text: Option A gives a certain profit of $50,000. Option B gives a profit of $120,000 if demand is strong and a loss of $20,000 if demand is weak. Above what probability of strong demand would Option B have the higher expected value?
questions.explanation: Let p be the probability of strong demand. EV of B = 120,000p - 20,000(1 - p) = 140,000p - 20,000. Setting this equal to 50,000 gives 140,000p = 70,000, so p = 0.50. Above this probability, B's expected value exceeds the certain $50,000.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the expected value of perfect information is correct?

options.A: It is the maximum amount that should be paid for information that predicts the outcome with certainty
options.B: It is always equal to the expected value of the best decision without information
options.C: It can be negative if the information leads to a different decision
options.D: It equals the value of imperfect information in all cases

questions.explanation: EVPI = EV with perfect information - EV without information. It sets a ceiling on what a decision-maker should pay for a forecast, since no information can be worth more than perfect information. It cannot be negative, and imperfect information is normally worth less.

questions.topic: Budgetary systems and types of budget
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the main criticism of incremental budgeting?

options.A: It requires every activity to be justified from a zero base
options.B: It is too time-consuming and expensive to prepare
options.C: It is updated continuously by adding a new period as each period ends
options.D: It tends to carry forward past inefficiencies and slack into the new budget

questions.explanation: Incremental budgeting takes last year's figures and adjusts them for expected changes, so existing inefficiencies and wasteful spending are rarely questioned. Justifying everything from zero describes ZBB, and continuous updating describes rolling budgets. Incremental budgeting is actually quick and cheap to prepare.

questions.topic: Budgetary systems and types of budget
questions.question_text: Under zero-based budgeting, what is a decision package?

options.A: A summary of last year's actual results adjusted for inflation
options.B: A set of budget targets agreed between head office and divisions
options.C: A document describing an activity, its costs and benefits, and alternative levels of service, which is ranked against other packages
options.D: A computer model used to flex the budget for the actual level of activity

questions.explanation: In ZBB each activity is described in a decision package setting out its purpose, costs, benefits and alternative ways or levels of performing it. Packages are ranked and resources are allocated to the highest-ranked packages until the budget is exhausted.

questions.topic: Budgetary systems and types of budget
questions.question_text: For which of the following types of cost is zero-based budgeting most likely to be useful?

options.A: Direct material costs that vary with production volume
options.B: Discretionary costs, such as staff training and advertising
options.C: Depreciation on factory buildings
options.D: Rent payable under a long-term lease

questions.explanation: ZBB is most useful where spending is discretionary and there is no clear link between input and output, such as training, advertising or research. Material costs are driven by output, and depreciation and lease rent are committed costs that cannot easily be changed in the short term.

questions.topic: Budgetary systems and types of budget
questions.question_text: A company prepares a 12-month budget. At the end of each month, it adds a budget for the same month of the following year and revises the remaining months. Which type of budget is this, and when is it most useful?

options.A: An incremental budget, most useful when operations are stable
options.B: A zero-based budget, most useful for discretionary costs
options.C: A rolling budget, most useful when the business environment is uncertain or changing quickly
options.D: A fixed budget, most useful for controlling variable costs

questions.explanation: A rolling (continuous) budget always covers a full period ahead by adding a new period as one expires, so plans reflect current conditions. This is particularly valuable where conditions change rapidly and an annual budget would soon become out of date. Its drawback is the time and cost of frequent revision.

questions.topic: Budgetary systems and types of budget
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a principle of the 'beyond budgeting' model?

options.A: Setting fixed annual targets that are agreed a year in advance
options.B: Allocating resources once a year through the annual budget
options.C: Using relative performance targets, such as benchmarks against competitors, instead of fixed annual targets
options.D: Centralising decision-making at head office to improve control

questions.explanation: Beyond budgeting argues that fixed annual budgets cause dysfunctional behaviour. It favours relative, flexible targets, resources made available on demand, decentralised decision-making and frequent rolling forecasts separate from performance evaluation.

questions.topic: Budgetary systems and types of budget
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a recognised disadvantage of participative (bottom-up) budgeting?

options.A: Managers are less motivated because the budget is imposed on them
options.B: Managers may build budgetary slack into their budgets to make targets easier to achieve
options.C: Budgets take less time to prepare than imposed budgets
options.D: Local managers' knowledge is ignored in setting targets

questions.explanation: When managers set their own budgets, they may overstate costs or understate revenues to create slack and make targets easier to meet. Participation generally improves motivation and uses local knowledge, but it takes longer than an imposed approach.

questions.topic: Budgetary systems and types of budget
questions.question_text: The original budget for 10,000 units included: variable costs $60,000; semi-variable costs $35,000 (of which $15,000 is fixed); and fixed costs $40,000. Actual output was 12,000 units. What is the total flexed budget cost?
questions.explanation: Variable cost per unit = $60,000 / 10,000 = $6; flexed = 12,000 x $6 = $72,000. Semi-variable: variable element $20,000 / 10,000 = $2 per unit, so 12,000 x $2 = $24,000 plus $15,000 fixed = $39,000. Fixed costs stay at $40,000. Total = $72,000 + $39,000 + $40,000 = $151,000.

questions.topic: Budgetary systems and types of budget
questions.question_text: A manager compares the latest forecast of the year's results with the annual target and takes corrective action before the year end to close an expected shortfall. What type of control is this?

options.A: Feedback control
options.B: Post-completion audit
options.C: Incremental control
options.D: Feedforward control

questions.explanation: Feedforward control compares forecast outcomes with targets so that action can be taken before deviations occur. Feedback control compares actual results with the budget after the event and corrects future performance.

questions.topic: Budgetary systems and types of budget
questions.question_text: Hopwood identified three styles of using budget information to evaluate managers. Under which style is a manager judged mainly on the ability to meet the budget in the short term, with little regard to other measures?

options.A: Profit-conscious style
options.B: Non-accounting style
options.C: Participative style
options.D: Budget-constrained style

questions.explanation: In the budget-constrained style, meeting short-term budget targets is the main criterion, which can cause stress and manipulation of data. The profit-conscious style focuses on long-term effectiveness, and the non-accounting style places little emphasis on budget data. 'Participative' describes how budgets are set, not one of Hopwood's evaluation styles.

questions.question_text: The first unit of a new product took 100 hours to make. An 80% learning curve applies. What is the cumulative average time per unit when 8 units have been produced?

options.A: 64.0 hours
options.B: 409.6 hours
options.C: 40.0 hours
options.D: 51.2 hours

questions.explanation: Each time cumulative output doubles, the cumulative average time falls to 80% of its previous value. 1 unit: 100 hours; 2 units: 80; 4 units: 64; 8 units: 51.2 hours. Total time for 8 units = 8 x 51.2 = 409.6 hours.

questions.question_text: The first unit of a product took 50 hours. An 85% learning curve applies, and the learning index is b = log 0.85 / log 2 = -0.2345 (to four decimal places). How long will the 20th unit take to produce (to one decimal place)?

options.A: 24.8 hours
options.B: 495.4 hours
options.C: 26.1 hours
options.D: 19.1 hours

questions.explanation: Using y = ax^b: cumulative average for 20 units = 50 x 20^-0.2345 = 24.767 hours, so total time = 20 x 24.767 = 495.35 hours. Cumulative average for 19 units = 50 x 19^-0.2345 = 25.067 hours, so total = 19 x 25.067 = 476.27 hours. Time for the 20th unit = 495.35 - 476.27 = 19.08, which is 19.1 hours to one decimal place (the unrounded index gives 19.08 as well). 24.8 hours is the cumulative average, 495.4 hours the cumulative total, and 26.1 hours the 16-unit average (50 x 0.85^4).

questions.question_text: The first batch of a new product took 200 hours. The first four batches took a total of 512 hours. What learning rate is being experienced?
questions.explanation: Cumulative average time for 4 batches = 512 / 4 = 128 hours. Four batches is two doublings from one, so 200 x r^2 = 128, giving r^2 = 0.64 and r = 0.80, an 80% learning rate.

questions.question_text: In which of the following situations is a learning curve most likely to apply?

options.A: A highly automated process where machines set the pace of work
options.B: A labour-intensive assembly process for a new, complex product, with a stable workforce and continuous production
options.C: A long-established product whose workers have made it for many years
options.D: A process where there are long breaks between production runs and high staff turnover

questions.explanation: Learning effects arise when a new task is repeated by people who retain what they have learned. They are strongest in labour-intensive, complex, early-stage production with continuity. Machine-paced work, mature products and frequent breaks or staff turnover limit or eliminate the learning effect.

questions.question_text: Total production costs were $74,000 at an activity level of 12,000 units and $102,000 at 20,000 units. Using the high-low method, what is the expected total cost at 17,000 units?

Total costs were $61,000 at 10,000 units and $93,000 at 18,000 units. Fixed costs increase by $8,000 when activity exceeds 15,000 units; the $93,000 includes this step. Using the high-low method, what is the expected total cost at 16,000 units?

A company uses linear regression (y = a + bx) to estimate overhead costs (y, $000) from machine hours (x, 000 hours). From five observations: n = 5, sum of x = 50, sum of y = 500, sum of xy = 5,240 and sum of x squared = 540. Using b = (n sum xy - sum x sum y) / (n sum x^2 - (sum x)^2) and a = (sum y / n) - b(sum x / n), what is the forecast overhead cost when 15,000 machine hours are worked?
The correlation coefficient between advertising spend and sales volume has been calculated as 0.9. What proportion of the variation in sales volume is explained by variation in advertising spend?
questions.explanation: The coefficient of determination equals r squared = 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.81. Therefore 81% of the variation in sales volume is explained by the variation in advertising spend; the remaining 19% is due to other factors.

questions.question_text: In the learning curve formula y = ax^b, b = log r / log 2. What is the value of b for a 90% learning curve (to three decimal places)?
questions.explanation: b = log 0.9 / log 2 = -0.0458 / 0.3010 = -0.152. The same result is obtained using natural logs, because the ratio of logs does not depend on the base.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a limitation of the high-low method of cost estimation?

options.A: It requires complex statistical software to calculate
options.B: It uses only the highest and lowest activity observations, which may not be representative of normal conditions
options.C: It cannot separate a cost into fixed and variable elements
options.D: It considers every observation in the data set equally

questions.explanation: The high-low method is simple and separates fixed and variable elements, but it relies on just two observations. If either is unusual, the estimate will be distorted. Regression analysis uses all data points and is therefore usually more reliable.

questions.question_text: Which type of standard assumes perfect operating conditions, with no allowance for wastage, idle time or machine breakdowns?

options.A: Ideal standard
options.B: Attainable standard
options.C: Current standard
options.D: Basic standard

questions.explanation: An ideal standard can only be achieved under perfect conditions and makes no allowance for normal losses or inefficiencies. Attainable standards allow for normal losses, current standards reflect present conditions, and basic standards are left unchanged over long periods for trend analysis.

questions.question_text: A company bought and used 4,200 kg of material at a total cost of $23,100. The standard price is $5.20 per kg and the standard usage is 4 kg per unit. Actual output was 1,000 units. What are the material price and usage variances?

options.A: Price $1,260 favourable; usage $1,040 adverse
options.B: Price $1,260 adverse; usage $1,040 favourable
options.C: Price $1,260 adverse; usage $1,040 adverse
options.D: Price $1,260 adverse; usage $1,100 adverse

questions.explanation: Price variance = $23,100 - (4,200 x $5.20) = $23,100 - $21,840 = $1,260 adverse. Standard quantity for 1,000 units = 4,000 kg. Usage variance = (4,000 - 4,200) x $5.20 = $1,040 adverse. Both are adverse because more was paid per kg and more kg were used than standard.

questions.question_text:
Product W is made by mixing two materials. The standard input to produce 9 kg of W is 6 kg of D at $4 per kg and 4 kg of E at $7 per kg. Last month, 2,900 kg of D and 2,100 kg of E were used, and 4,410 kg of W were produced.
What is the total materials mix variance?

options.A: $300 favourable
options.B: $400 favourable
options.C: $300 adverse
options.D: $520 adverse

questions.explanation: Total actual input = 5,000 kg. In standard mix: D 3,000 kg and E 2,000 kg. D: (3,000 - 2,900) x $4 = $400 favourable. E: (2,000 - 2,100) x $7 = $700 adverse. Total mix variance = $300 adverse, because proportionately more of the expensive material E was used.

questions.question_text:
Product W is made by mixing two materials. The standard input to produce 9 kg of W is 6 kg of D at $4 per kg and 4 kg of E at $7 per kg. Last month, 2,900 kg of D and 2,100 kg of E were used, and 4,410 kg of W were produced.
What is the total materials yield variance?

options.A: $520 favourable
options.B: $520 adverse
options.C: $578 adverse
options.D: $700 adverse

questions.explanation: Standard cost per kg of input = ((6 x $4) + (4 x $7)) / 10 = $5.20. Standard input for 4,410 kg of output = 4,410 / 9 x 10 = 4,900 kg. Actual input = 5,000 kg. Yield variance = (4,900 - 5,000) x $5.20 = $520 adverse.

questions.question_text: A production manager changes the mix of ingredients in a process to use a higher proportion of a cheaper material. Which combination of variances is most likely to result?

options.A: An adverse mix variance and a favourable yield variance
options.B: A favourable mix variance and an adverse yield variance
options.C: A favourable mix variance and a favourable yield variance
options.D: An adverse price variance and a favourable yield variance

questions.explanation: Using more of the cheaper material reduces the standard cost of the actual input, giving a favourable mix variance. However, the cheaper mix may produce less output per kg of input or lower quality, leading to an adverse yield variance. The variances are interdependent and should be assessed together.

questions.question_text:
Mu Co sells products G and H. Budgeted sales were 3,000 units of G and 2,000 units of H. Standard contribution is $10 per unit for G and $20 per unit for H. Actual sales were 3,600 units of G and 1,900 units of H.
What is the total sales mix contribution variance?

options.A: $3,000 adverse
options.B: $3,000 favourable
options.C: $7,000 favourable
options.D: $6,000 adverse

questions.explanation: Actual total sales = 5,500 units. In budgeted mix (60:40): G 3,300 and H 2,200. G: (3,600 - 3,300) x $10 = $3,000 favourable. H: (1,900 - 2,200) x $20 = $6,000 adverse. Mix variance = $3,000 adverse, because the mix shifted towards G, which earns less contribution per unit.

questions.question_text:
Mu Co sells products G and H. Budgeted sales were 3,000 units of G and 2,000 units of H. Standard contribution is $10 per unit for G and $20 per unit for H. Actual sales were 3,600 units of G and 1,900 units of H.
What is the total sales quantity contribution variance?

options.A: $7,000 adverse
options.B: $4,000 favourable
options.C: $7,000 favourable
options.D: $7,500 favourable

questions.explanation: Weighted average standard contribution per unit = ((3,000 x $10) + (2,000 x $20)) / 5,000 = $14. Quantity variance = (5,500 - 5,000) x $14 = $7,000 favourable. Check: mix $3,000 A + quantity $7,000 F = total sales volume variance $4,000 F.

questions.question_text: The standard price of a material was set at $8 per kg. During the period, a worldwide shortage meant the market price rose, and management agreed that a realistic standard would have been $9 per kg. The company bought 6,000 kg at $9.40 per kg. What are the material price planning and operational variances?

options.A: Planning $2,400 adverse; operational $6,000 adverse
options.B: Planning $6,000 favourable; operational $2,400 adverse
options.C: Planning $8,400 adverse; operational $0
options.D: Planning $6,000 adverse; operational $2,400 adverse

questions.explanation: Planning variance = (original standard - revised standard) x actual quantity = ($8 - $9) x 6,000 = $6,000 adverse; this is outside the purchasing manager's control. Operational variance = (revised standard - actual price) x actual quantity = ($9 - $9.40) x 6,000 = $2,400 adverse. Together they equal the total price variance of $8,400 adverse.

questions.question_text: The standard labour time is 2 hours per unit at $12 per hour. Following new safety regulations that were not foreseen when the standard was set, a realistic standard would have been 2.5 hours per unit. Output was 1,800 units and 4,300 hours were worked. What is the labour efficiency operational variance?

options.A: $2,400 favourable
options.B: $10,800 adverse
options.C: $8,400 adverse
options.D: $2,400 adverse

questions.explanation: Revised standard hours for actual output = 1,800 x 2.5 = 4,500 hours. Operational efficiency variance = (4,500 - 4,300) x $12 = $2,400 favourable. The planning variance is (3,600 - 4,500) x $12 = $10,800 adverse, giving a total efficiency variance of $8,400 adverse.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a recognised problem with separating variances into planning and operational elements?

options.A: Managers may try to claim that adverse variances are due to planning errors outside their control
options.B: It always makes operational variances appear worse than the total variance
