options.C: It removes the need to set standards at the start of the period
options.D: It can only be applied to sales variances and not to cost variances

questions.explanation: Revised standards are set with hindsight and involve judgement, so managers have an incentive to argue that poor results are planning (uncontrollable) issues. Establishing a realistic revised standard can also be time-consuming. Planning and operational analysis can be applied to sales, material, labour and overhead variances.

questions.question_text: A purchasing manager buys a cheaper, lower-quality grade of material than standard. Which combination of variances is most likely to arise?

options.A: An adverse material price variance and a favourable material usage variance
options.B: A favourable material price variance and a favourable labour efficiency variance
options.C: An adverse material price variance and an adverse labour rate variance
options.D: A favourable material price variance and an adverse material usage variance

questions.explanation: Paying less per kg gives a favourable price variance, but lower-quality material is likely to cause more wastage and rejects, giving an adverse usage variance. It may also slow production, causing an adverse labour efficiency variance. This illustrates the interdependence of variances.

questions.question_text: A company's standard selling price for product T is $50 per unit. During the period it sold 1,900 units at an average price of $48 per unit. What is the sales price variance?

options.A: $3,800 adverse
options.B: $3,800 favourable
options.C: $4,000 adverse
options.D: $2,000 adverse

questions.explanation: Sales price variance = (actual price - standard price) x actual units sold = ($48 - $50) x 1,900 = $3,800 adverse. It is adverse because each unit was sold for less than the standard price, and it is based on actual, not budgeted, quantity.

questions.question_text: A company using a balanced scorecard measures 'the percentage of revenue generated by products launched in the last two years'. Under which perspective would this measure most appropriately fall?

options.A: Financial perspective
options.B: Learning and growth (innovation) perspective
options.C: Customer perspective
options.D: Internal business process perspective

questions.explanation: The learning and growth perspective asks whether the organisation can continue to improve and create value, including through innovation. Revenue from new products measures the success of innovation. The financial perspective would use measures such as ROCE, and the customer perspective measures such as market share or satisfaction.

questions.question_text: In Fitzgerald and Moon's building block model, which of the following is one of the three characteristics that the 'standards' building block requires?

options.A: Clarity
options.B: Flexibility
options.C: Competitiveness
options.D: Ownership

questions.explanation: The standards block requires ownership (managers accept the standards), achievability (they can be reached) and equity (they are fair across business units). Clarity belongs to the rewards block, along with motivation and controllability. Flexibility and competitiveness are dimensions of performance.

questions.question_text: In Fitzgerald and Moon's building block model, the dimensions of performance are divided into results and determinants. Which of the following is a RESULTS dimension?

options.A: Quality of service
options.B: Flexibility
options.C: Competitiveness
options.D: Resource utilisation

questions.explanation: The results dimensions are financial performance and competitiveness; they show the outcome of past decisions. The determinants are quality of service, flexibility, resource utilisation and innovation, which drive future results.

questions.question_text: A company has current assets of $240,000, of which inventory is $90,000, and current liabilities of $150,000. What is its quick (acid test) ratio?
questions.explanation: Quick ratio = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities = ($240,000 - $90,000) / $150,000 = 1.0. The current ratio, which includes inventory, would be 1.6.

questions.question_text: A company has trade receivables of $82,000. Annual sales are $800,000, of which $730,000 are on credit and $70,000 are for cash. What is the trade receivables collection period (using a 365-day year)?

options.A: 37.4 days
options.B: 40.4 days
options.C: 36.9 days
options.D: 41 days

questions.explanation: Receivables collection period = (trade receivables / credit sales) x 365 = ($82,000 / $730,000) x 365 = 41 days. Only credit sales create receivables: using total sales gives 37.4 days, a 360-day year gives 40.4 days, and both errors together give 36.9 days.

questions.question_text: A company has operating profit of $180,000, revenue of $900,000 and capital employed of $1,200,000. What is its return on capital employed (ROCE)?
questions.explanation: ROCE = operating profit / capital employed = $180,000 / $1,200,000 = 15%. This equals the operating profit margin (20%) multiplied by asset turnover (0.75 times).

questions.question_text: A company's operating profit margin is 12% and its ROCE is 18%. Revenue is $3,000,000. What is the company's capital employed?
questions.explanation: ROCE = margin x asset turnover, so asset turnover = 18% / 12% = 1.5 times. Capital employed = revenue / asset turnover = $3,000,000 / 1.5 = $2,000,000. Check: operating profit = 12% x $3,000,000 = $360,000, and $360,000 / $2,000,000 = 18%.

questions.question_text: A public hospital reports that its cost per patient treated has fallen while the number and quality of treatments have been maintained. Which element of value for money does this best demonstrate?

options.A: Economy
options.B: Efficiency
options.C: Effectiveness
options.D: Equity

questions.explanation: Efficiency is the relationship between outputs and inputs, so a lower cost per patient treated shows more output per $ of resource. Economy concerns obtaining inputs at the lowest cost, and effectiveness concerns achieving objectives or outcomes.

questions.question_text: A local government wants to measure the EFFECTIVENESS of its adult literacy programme. Which of the following measures is most appropriate?

options.A: The cost per hour of tutoring purchased
options.B: The number of participants taught per tutor
options.C: The amount spent on teaching materials compared with budget
options.D: The percentage of participants who reach the target reading standard

questions.explanation: Effectiveness is about whether the programme achieves its objectives, here improving literacy, so the proportion reaching the target standard is the best measure. Cost per tutoring hour measures economy, participants per tutor measures efficiency, and spend against budget is a financial control measure.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a particular difficulty in measuring the performance of not-for-profit organisations?

options.A: They have no costs that can be measured
options.B: Their performance can be fully captured by profit
options.C: They often have multiple objectives whose outputs are hard to quantify in money terms
options.D: They are not accountable to any stakeholders

questions.explanation: Not-for-profit organisations usually pursue several, sometimes conflicting, non-financial objectives, such as health, education or social outcomes, which are difficult to measure and value. Profit is not their aim, so value-for-money measures are used, and they are accountable to many stakeholders such as funders and the public.

questions.question_text: A divisional manager cuts the staff training budget and delays machine maintenance in order to meet this year's profit target. Which of the following is most likely to reduce this kind of behaviour?

options.A: Increasing the bonus linked solely to annual profit
options.B: Assessing performance using a range of financial and non-financial measures, including long-term indicators
options.C: Evaluating the manager only on monthly cost variances
options.D: Removing all performance targets from the reward system

questions.explanation: Cutting discretionary spending to boost short-term profit is short-termism. Using a broader set of measures, such as staff development, quality and customer satisfaction, and linking rewards to longer-term performance, reduces the incentive. Stronger links to annual profit or to short-term cost variances would make the problem worse.

questions.question_text:
Division D has capital employed of $4,000,000 and controllable profit of $640,000. The company's cost of capital is 12%.
What is the division's return on investment (ROI)?
questions.explanation: ROI = controllable profit / capital employed = $640,000 / $4,000,000 = 16%.

questions.question_text:
Division D has capital employed of $4,000,000 and controllable profit of $640,000. The company's cost of capital is 12%.
What is the division's residual income (RI)?
questions.explanation: Imputed interest = 12% x $4,000,000 = $480,000. RI = controllable profit - imputed interest = $640,000 - $480,000 = $160,000.

questions.question_text:
Division D has capital employed of $4,000,000 and controllable profit of $640,000. The company's cost of capital is 12%.
The divisional manager is considering a new project requiring investment of $500,000 and generating an annual controllable profit of $70,000. What would be the effect of accepting the project?

options.A: ROI would fall to 14.0% and RI would increase by $10,000
options.B: ROI would fall to 15.8% and RI would fall by $10,000
options.C: ROI would fall to 15.8% but RI would increase by $10,000
options.D: ROI would stay at 16% and RI would increase by $70,000

questions.explanation: New ROI = ($640,000 + $70,000) / ($4,000,000 + $500,000) = 15.8%, lower than the current 16%. Change in RI = $70,000 - (12% x $500,000) = $10,000 increase. A manager judged on ROI might reject a project that earns more than the cost of capital, which is a weakness of ROI.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a disadvantage of residual income compared with return on investment as a divisional performance measure?

options.A: It encourages managers to reject projects that earn more than the cost of capital
options.B: It is an absolute measure, so it does not allow easy comparison of divisions of different sizes
options.C: It ignores the cost of the capital tied up in the division
options.D: It cannot reflect different levels of risk across divisions

questions.explanation: RI is expressed in $, so larger divisions tend to report higher RI, making comparisons between divisions of different sizes difficult. ROI is the measure that can lead to rejecting worthwhile projects, and RI explicitly charges for capital and can use different rates for divisions with different risk.

questions.question_text: A division's assets are measured at net book value. If profits remain constant and no new assets are acquired, what will happen to the division's ROI over time?

options.A: It will increase as the assets depreciate
options.B: It will decrease as the assets depreciate
options.C: It will remain constant
options.D: It will become negative once the assets are fully depreciated

questions.explanation: As assets depreciate, their net book value and therefore capital employed fall. With constant profit, ROI rises over time even though performance has not improved. This can discourage managers from replacing old assets, since new investment would reduce ROI.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a key objective of a transfer pricing system?

options.A: Maximising the profit of the supplying division at the expense of the receiving division
options.B: Ensuring that every transfer is made at full cost
options.C: Encouraging divisional managers to make decisions that are in the best interests of the company as a whole
options.D: Removing the autonomy of divisional managers

questions.explanation: A good transfer pricing system should promote goal congruence, allow fair performance evaluation of each division and preserve divisional autonomy. Maximising one division's profit at another's expense, or always using full cost, can lead to dysfunctional decisions.

questions.question_text: Division S makes a component with a variable cost of $30 and a full cost of $42 per unit. It has spare capacity and there is no external market for the component. Division R can buy an equivalent component from an outside supplier for $55. Within what range should the transfer price lie to encourage goal-congruent decisions?

options.A: Between $30 and $55
options.B: Between $42 and $55
options.C: Between $30 and $42
options.D: At or above $55, the external supplier's price

questions.explanation: With spare capacity, the supplying division's opportunity cost is zero, so the minimum transfer price is its variable cost of $30. The maximum the receiving division would pay is the external price of $55. Any price in this range should lead both managers to favour the internal transfer. Using full cost ($42) as the floor ignores the spare capacity, and a price above $55 would push Division R to buy externally.

questions.question_text: Division S makes a component with a variable cost of $30 per unit. It is working at full capacity and sells all its output externally at $50 per unit, incurring selling costs of $2 per unit that would be avoided on internal transfers. What is the minimum transfer price that Division S should accept for transfers to Division R?
questions.explanation: Minimum transfer price = marginal cost + opportunity cost. The opportunity cost is the contribution lost on an external sale: $50 - $2 - $30 = $18. Minimum price = $30 + $18 = $48. Equivalently, the external price less the selling costs saved: $50 - $2 = $48.

questions.question_text: Under a two-part tariff transfer pricing system, how are transfers charged?

options.A: At full cost plus a percentage mark-up on every unit
options.B: At market price for the supplying division and at marginal cost for the receiving division
options.C: At marginal cost per unit, plus a fixed fee each period to cover the supplying division's fixed costs and a profit
options.D: At a price negotiated afresh for each individual transfer

questions.explanation: A two-part tariff charges units at marginal cost, so the receiving division makes decisions using the true incremental cost, plus a fixed periodic fee so the supplier recovers fixed costs and earns a profit. Recording different prices for each division describes dual pricing.

questions.question_text: Division S transfers a component to Division R at full cost plus 20%. Which problem is most likely to arise?

options.A: Division S will never cover its fixed costs
options.B: Division R will always buy more units than is optimal for the company
options.C: Division R treats Division S's fixed costs and mark-up as variable costs, and may reject orders that would be profitable for the company
options.D: The transfer price will always equal the external market price

questions.explanation: To the receiving division the whole transfer price is a variable cost, even though part of it covers fixed costs and profit of the supplier. Division R may therefore turn down sales whose price exceeds the company's true marginal cost but not the inflated transfer price, which is not goal congruent.
